items.readable_text:
Content:
In a previous lesson, we used [MATH: \max] and [MATH: \min] to talk about the largest and smallest values a function can take on a set.

Content:
In this lesson, we learn two closely related pieces of notation:

Content:
- [MATH: \max] and [MATH: \min] return the best (largest/smallest) function value.
- [MATH: \arg\max] and [MATH: \arg\min] return the input value (the "argument") where that best value occurs.

Content:
For example, let [MATH: S = \{1,2,3\}] and suppose
[MATH: f(1)=4,\qquad f(2)=7,\qquad f(3)=6.]
Then the largest function value is [MATH: 7,] and it occurs when [MATH: x=2{:}]
[MATH: max_(x ∈ S)f(x)|= 7,; \arg max_(x ∈ S)f(x)|= 2.]

Content:
Similarly, [MATH: \min_{x \in S} f(x)] is the smallest function value, and [MATH: \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x)] is an input where that smallest value occurs.

Content:
Watch out! Sometimes the best value occurs at more than one input. In that case, we need to clarify what [MATH: \arg\max] (or [MATH: \arg\min]) means. We will handle this after we practice the basic case.

sections.normalized_html: Let [MATH: S=\{-1,0,2,4\}] and suppose [MATH: f(-1)=3,\qquad f(0)=-2,\qquad f(2)=5,\qquad f(4)=1.] Compute the following: [MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \arg\max_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \min_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x).]
sections.readable_text:
Let [MATH: S=\{-1,0,2,4\}] and suppose
[MATH: f(-1)=3,\qquad f(0)=-2,\qquad f(2)=5,\qquad f(4)=1.]
Compute the following:
[MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \arg\max_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \min_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x).]

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that

  • [MATH: \max\limits_{x \in S} f(x)] is the largest output value, while

  • [MATH: \arg\max\limits_{x \in S} f(x)] is an input in [MATH: S] where that largest output occurs.

On the other hand,

  • [MATH: \min\limits_{x \in S} f(x)] is the smallest output value, while

  • [MATH: \arg\min\limits_{x \in S} f(x)] is an input in [MATH: S] where that smallest output occurs.

The outputs of [MATH: f] on [MATH: S] are [MATH: 3,\qquad -2,\qquad 5,\qquad 1.] The largest output is [MATH: 5,] and it occurs at [MATH: x=2.] Therefore, [MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x)=5, \qquad \arg\max_{x \in S} f(x)=2.]

Similarly, the smallest output is [MATH: -2,] and it occurs at [MATH: x=0.] Therefore, [MATH: \min_{x \in S} f(x)=-2, \qquad \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x)=0.]

items.title: Writing and Reading Formal Notation

sections.normalized_html: Let [MATH: S] be a set and let [MATH: f] be a real-valued function on [MATH: S.] Consider the expression [MATH: x^*=\arg\max_{x \in S} f(x).] What does this statement mean in words? Also, what does [MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x)] represent?
sections.readable_text:
Let [MATH: S] be a set and let [MATH: f] be a real-valued function on [MATH: S.] Consider the expression
[MATH: x^*=\arg\max_{x \in S} f(x).]
What does this statement mean in words? Also, what does [MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x)] represent?

sections.normalized_html:
The expression [MATH: x^*=\arg\max_{x \in S} f(x)] means that:

  • [MATH: x^*] is an input value in [MATH: S.]

  • Among all [MATH: x \in S,] the value [MATH: f(x^*)] is as large as possible.

In other words, [MATH: x^*] is a choice of input where [MATH: f] attains its largest value on [MATH: S.]

By contrast, [MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x)] is not an input. It is the largest function value that [MATH: f] attains on [MATH: S.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In a previous lesson, we used [MATH: \max] and [MATH: \min] to talk about the largest and smallest values a function can take on a set.

Content:
In this lesson, we learn two closely related pieces of notation:

Content:
- [MATH: \max] and [MATH: \min] return the best (largest/smallest) function value.
- [MATH: \arg\max] and [MATH: \arg\min] return the input value (the "argument") where that best value occurs.

Content:
For example, let [MATH: S = \{1,2,3\}] and suppose
[MATH: f(1)=4,\qquad f(2)=7,\qquad f(3)=6.]
Then the largest function value is [MATH: 7,] and it occurs when [MATH: x=2{:}]
[MATH: max_(x ∈ S)f(x)|= 7,; \arg max_(x ∈ S)f(x)|= 2.]

Content:
Similarly, [MATH: \min_{x \in S} f(x)] is the smallest function value, and [MATH: \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x)] is an input where that smallest value occurs.

Content:
Watch out! Sometimes the best value occurs at more than one input. In that case, we need to clarify what [MATH: \arg\max] (or [MATH: \arg\min]) means. We will handle this after we practice the basic case.

---

Item 2 — Example: Distinguishing Between Max/Min and Argmax/Argmin

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: S=\{-1,0,2,4\}] and suppose
[MATH: f(-1)=3,\qquad f(0)=-2,\qquad f(2)=5,\qquad f(4)=1.]
Compute the following:
[MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \arg\max_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \min_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that

- [MATH: \max\limits_{x \in S} f(x)] is the largest output value, while
- [MATH: \arg\max\limits_{x \in S} f(x)] is an input in [MATH: S] where that largest output occurs.

On the other hand,

- [MATH: \min\limits_{x \in S} f(x)] is the smallest output value, while
- [MATH: \arg\min\limits_{x \in S} f(x)] is an input in [MATH: S] where that smallest output occurs.

The outputs of [MATH: f] on [MATH: S] are
[MATH: 3,\qquad -2,\qquad 5,\qquad 1.]
The largest output is [MATH: 5,] and it occurs at [MATH: x=2.] Therefore,
[MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x)=5,
\qquad
\arg\max_{x \in S} f(x)=2.]

Similarly, the smallest output is [MATH: -2,] and it occurs at [MATH: x=0.] Therefore,
[MATH: \min_{x \in S} f(x)=-2,
\qquad
\arg\min_{x \in S} f(x)=0.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Argmax and Argmin With Ties

Content:
Sometimes a function attains its largest (or smallest) value at more than one input. In that case, there are multiple inputs that satisfy the definition of [MATH: \arg\max] (or [MATH: \arg\min]).

Content:
In this course, when a tie occurs, we report the set of all inputs where the maximum is achieved as follows:
[MATH: \arg\max_{x \in S} f(x) = {x \in S{:} f(x) = \max_{u \in S} f(u)}.]

Content:
Similarly, when a tie occurs, we report the set of all inputs where the minimum is achieved as follows:
[MATH: \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x) = {x \in S{:} f(x) = \min_{u \in S} f(u)}.]

Content:
The quantities [MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x)] and [MATH: \min_{x \in S} f(x)] are still single numbers.

---

Item 6 — Example: Computing Argmax and Argmin With Ties

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: S=\{-1,0,2,3\}] and suppose
[MATH: f(-1)=4,\qquad f(0)=1,\qquad f(2)=4,\qquad f(3)=2.]
Compute [MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x)] and [MATH: \arg\max_{x \in S} f(x).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that

- [MATH: \max\limits_{x \in S} f(x)] is the largest output value, while
- [MATH: \arg\max\limits_{x \in S} f(x)] is an input in [MATH: S] where that largest output occurs.

The output values are [MATH: 4,1,4,] and [MATH: 2.] The maximum output value is [MATH: 4.]

This maximum occurs at both [MATH: x=-1] and [MATH: x=2.] Therefore,
[MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x)=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{4}
\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad
\arg\max_{x \in S} f(x)=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\{-1,2\}}.]

Item 9 — Example: Writing and Reading Formal Notation

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: S] be a set and let [MATH: f] be a real-valued function on [MATH: S.] Consider the expression
[MATH: x^*=\arg\max_{x \in S} f(x).]
What does this statement mean in words? Also, what does [MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x)] represent?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The expression [MATH: x^*=\arg\max_{x \in S} f(x)] means that:

- [MATH: x^*] is an input value in [MATH: S.]
- Among all [MATH: x \in S,] the value [MATH: f(x^*)] is as large as possible.

In other words, [MATH: x^*] is a choice of input where [MATH: f] attains its largest value on [MATH: S.]

By contrast, [MATH: \max_{x \in S} f(x)] is not an input. It is the largest function value that [MATH: f] attains on [MATH: S.]
